batch_13.scope_rule_applied: A named offering built FOR unmanned aircraft or counter-UAS counts; a general-purpose product that somebody else put into a drone does not. This matches the already-verified component suppliers (Turkish Engine Industries, YellowScan, Volz Servos) and was needed because the queue reached a seam of large general-technology companies.
duplicates_of_already_verified_companies: Frankenberg Technologies -> Frankenburg Technologies (Estonia), already verified with the Mark I interceptor; the duplicate was misspelled and filed as United Kingdom
TUSAS -> Turkish Aerospace (TAI), already verified with seven products
Santa Barbara Sistemas -> GDELS-Santa Barbara Sistemas, already verified
Qioptiq (Excelitas) -> Teledyne Qioptiq (Teledyne completed the purchase in February 2025)
corrections_claude_made_against_research: Country: the researched canonical-parent country was REJECTED for six companies (Teledyne Qioptiq, PZL Mielec, Santa Barbara, Rotax, Axis, Odin Defence). Applying it would have moved six European companies out of the landscape scope. Operating country applied; parent recorded in the description.
Product ownership: Turkish Aerospace held records for Kizilelma and Akinci, which are Baykar aircraft. Both reassigned to Baykar, sources folded into Baykar's existing records.
GRIM Tech admitted despite a charity-entity caution; Defense News coverage and a trade-fair exhibitor listing establish a manufacturer.
EURENCO: the DEMON attribution the research could not confirm does carry a French trade source in the existing product record.
Seven large general-technology companies decided under the new scope rule: Ericsson and Deutsche Telekom admitted, Nordic Semiconductor, Axis, Rotax, Varjo, Eutelsat and OQ Technology excluded.
batch_13.known_issue_not_fixed: Baykar now holds 15 product rows for about 6 aircraft (Akinci/Akinci/Bayraktar Akinci, four Kizilelma spellings, TB2/Bayraktar TB2, TB3/Bayraktar TB3). Product-level duplication predates this batch.

batch_14.composition: All 9 remaining records with no data at all (exempted from the country cap, which held 9 of them back in Batch 13 because the blanks cluster in Ukraine), plus 31 records with a website or product but no description, capped at 5 per country.
instructions_rewritten: State the operating country of THIS company and name any parent group and its country separately. Do not replace the operating country with the parent country. (Batch 13 showed the previous canonical-parent question would have moved six European companies out of scope.)
Say whether the offering is built FOR unmanned aircraft or counter-UAS, or is a general-purpose product someone else put into a drone.
The duplicate question now names spelling variants and former names, not only subsidiaries.
The non-company list now includes investors and accelerators, and end users.

remaining_queue_profile.enrichment_runway: Batch 14 clears the last 9 blanks and 31 partials. About 40 records with no description remain after it, which is one more batch. The enrichment phase ends there; what follows must be either verifying the backlog on its merits or clearing the publication gap.

open_questions_for_human: Warhead and energetics scope: five companies (EURENCO, Odin Defence, TDW, Wolfram Europa, Teledyne Energetics). Unchanged by Batch 13.
Operator and services scope: five companies (Unmanned4you, Extensee, Team UAV, Eagle Eye Innovations, Randle Engineering). Unchanged by Batch 13.
229 companies with landscape status excluded or needs_review have publication_status live and are on xsonomy.com, up from 206 after Batch 12. Claude has changed no publication status.

New, from Batch 13: the component scope rule was applied without being asked for, because the queue reached large general-technology companies and the loop could not proceed without one. The rule is in the Batch 13 report. If Nazar disagrees, Ericsson and Deutsche Telekom come out and Nordic Semiconductor, Axis, Rotax, Varjo, Eutelsat and OQ Technology go in.
notes: The queue has moved past small unknown companies into large well-known ones with empty records, which changed the kind of judgement required: most calls this batch were scope and ownership, not evidence. Three of five duplicates were of already-verified companies, and the TUSAS merge exposed two Baykar aircraft filed under Turkish Aerospace.
